set.approach: Leave the car at a pullout on Moraine Lake Road a mile or two short of the Moraine Lake parking area, and follow the trail that climbs the grassy slope north of the road toward the foot of the ridge. The grass gives way to talus, then a third-class ridge, then several hundred feet of moderate scrambling to a broad shoulder. That shoulder sits at the base of the Big Step, where the roped climbing begins with two or three pitches of steep 5.6.
set.descent_text: Most parties continue over the summit and walk down the southwest ridge, the heavily used scramble route, which leads back to the Moraine Lake area. Carry boots and an axe for the corniced summit ridge and any snow on the way down, and allow time for the long walk out along the lake road or shuttle.
hazards: Grizzly activity in the Moraine Lake area can bring a minimum party size of four on the approach and descent trails; check current restrictions before leaving
Loose rock throughout, with protection that is awkward to place
Soft cornices and possible crevasses along the summit ridge, unstable on warm days
Snow on the ledge traverses and in the upper half of the right-hand gully early in the season

set.overview: The classic line on the Devils Thumb, a granite spire rising from the Stikine Icecap on the Alaska-British Columbia border. It climbs the glacier and snow slopes south of the peak to a snow crest called the Hog's Back, goes up a face of moderate couloirs and slabs to a notch in the east ridge, then follows the ridge crest over a gendarme, a short steep headwall and a near-vertical exit face to the summit block. It is a grade V outing of about 3,000 feet, with rock climbing up to 5.8+ and serious weather.
set.approach: The Thumb is reached by helicopter from Petersburg, a short flight that often waits days for weather, or by a much longer boat-and-foot trip. Parties land on or near the Stikine Icecap and set a camp on the broad glacier directly south of the peak, below the southeast face. From camp, climb gradually steepening snow slopes and cross the bergschrund to reach the Hog's Back, then traverse east along it to the steep snow couloirs that lead up the face.
set.descent_text: Reverse the route along the ridge to the Rappel Notch and rappel the southeast face with double-rope stations, rigging your own anchors where none exist. Lower down, the bergschrund may need one more rappel from the rocks at its edge before the easy walk back across the glacier to camp.
hazards: Heavy precipitation and fast-changing storms are the norm on the Thumb, and clear windows can be short
The bergschrund and steep snow slopes below the Hog's Back
Wet, mossy rock on the short headwall, and a hard gendarme and near-vertical exit face on the crest
Crevassed icefall travel on the glacier approach from the landing area to the base of the peak

review.notes: Rappel count left out (only one page states it). Season, gain and distance skipped: no figures found. Peak-level hazards (weather, icefall approach) come from accounts of other lines on the same peak.

set.descent_text: Rappel the route, using two 60 m ropes. The upper part has fixed stations, but below the big bivouac ledge the rappel line leaves the climbing route and goes down the open face, where stations are hard to find and ropes snag on knobs. Keep out of the chimney: rappelling into it means a long, slow descent. Carry extra slings and webbing because fixed stations get sparse higher up.
hazards: The third pitch is often wet and slippery, around 5.10a when dry
Hard-to-find rappel stations on the open face, with ropes that snag on knobs
Rappelling into the chimney leads to long rope jams and a slow retreat
Weather in the Cirque changes quickly and afternoon storms are common; start early
Remote and exposed, with park pre-registration required to enter and leave

set.overview: The easiest route to the top of Devils Tower and the most popular line on it, about 500 feet over six pitches. It follows the Leaning Column and a series of cracks on the south side, with off-width and chimney moves, and finishes by crossing a broad meadow-like ledge near the top. The crux is the second pitch crack, where a big cam is useful, and the final jump traverse can be avoided by a short direct crack.
set.approach: Register at the visitor center, then take the paved Tower Trail around the base to the south side. Either turn up a faint trail and easy ramp to the foot of the Leaning Column, or continue along the trail to a clear path that reaches the base of the tower in about five minutes, climb an easy crack, and traverse left on fourth-class ground to the column.
set.descent_text: From the summit, walk back to the top of the direct finish crack and downclimb a few feet to the first rappel station, which drops into the meadow ledge near the jump traverse. Downclimb right to the bolts below, then make three more rappels down the Bowling Alley, which lies a few hundred feet to the right of the climb. All rappels need two ropes; rappel over the nose of each pillar rather than in the crack to avoid a stuck rope. Sign out at the visitor center afterward.
hazards: Loose rock on the flake crack pitch
Ropes jam if rappels run down the cracks instead of over the pillar noses
Heavy traffic on the route; start at first light or late afternoon if you are fast
Seasonal falcon closures on some faces, and a voluntary request to skip the tower in June

set.overview: A long granite buttress of about 1,500 feet and eleven pitches on the south side of Mount Moran, reached by canoe across two lakes. The climbing is sustained crack work with a double pendulum and a long hand traverse high up, and a short aid section that has been freed at a much higher grade. The buttress ends in a bowl roughly a third of the way up the peak; continuing to the summit adds easier scrambling and an exposed 5.6 ridge.
hazards: Loose stone in the descent chutes, plus a loose corner on the fifth pitch
Strong, sustained wind on the upper buttress, which makes aid and traverses harder
Grizzly bears have been seen in Leigh Canyon on the approach
Snow and ice in the bowl and gullies, particularly in snowy years or early in the season, call for axe and crampons
Easy to get lost on the approach pitches, and no running water in the bowl above

set.approach: Start at the Big Sandy trailhead, near 9,080 ft, and hike the Big Sandy Trail toward Jackass Pass, about 8 to 9 miles to the Cirque of the Towers. A climbers' trail that bypasses the loose slope below the pass leads around Arrowhead Lake into the upper cirque. Camp is usually near the lakes; from there it is about two more miles and 1,700 ft up to the base of the ridge, near the low point between Tiger Tower and Wolf's Head, reached by fifth-class cracks and ledges.
set.descent_text: Come off the summit down the west face by short rappels and loose downclimbing, then scramble a class 3 traverse to the saddle with the Overhanging Tower, where slings mark a final rappel onto loose scree. The scree leads down into the basin and back to camp about an hour from the saddle. A short class 4 section sits at the headwall above the saddle.
hazards: Serious exposure and tricky route-finding along the ridge, with many ups and downs between the north and south sides
Afternoon thunderstorms are common in the cirque; start early
Loose rock on the descent and grassy ledges that are slick when wet
A long day that can end in the dark, so carry a headlamp
Lonesome Lake water is not safe to drink, even filtered

review.notes: Rappel counts differ between the two descent accounts (about 4 vs fewer), so no count is given. Gain, distance and season skipped as optional for a long ridge with no stated window.
